display_title_he: עידוד חיסון נגד RSV בעקבות מקרה קשה
short_summary: A mother whose newborn daughter nearly died from a severe respiratory virus is urging pregnant women to get vaccinated.

sources.name: BBC News
sources.title: Mum told to 'prepare for worst' urges others to get respiratory illness vaccine

paragraphs: A mother in Wales whose newborn daughter contracted a potentially life-threatening respiratory illness is passionately urging other expectant mothers to ensure they receive the relevant vaccine. Jo Goldsmith recalled being instructed to prepare for the absolute worst after her infant daughter, Phoebe, fell seriously ill just days following her birth.

At the time of her pregnancy, the immunization was unavailable, yet Goldsmith stated firmly that she would have opted for it immediately. She explained that she would not wish any family to endure the trauma her household experienced during that period. Nerys Evans, the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, joined in prompting individuals to secure their vaccinations against Covid-19, influenza, and the respiratory syncytial virus prior to the arrival of the winter months.

According to the National Health Service, respiratory syncytial virus functions as a frequent catalyst for standard coughs and colds. Although most infections resolve independently without intervention, the pathogen can occasionally trigger severe medical complications for infants as well as older adults. Goldsmith, who works professionally as a children's nurse and health visitor located in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, noted that she recognized within days of Phoebe's birth four years ago that something was amiss.

The infant exhibited heavy congestion and began struggling with rapid breathing. Goldsmith brought her child to the hospital, where the situation rapidly escalated until medical staff confirmed a diagnosis of RSV-positive bronchiolitis on Christmas Eve. Phoebe's condition soon worsened significantly, leading to her admission into the high dependency unit. Although her medical background as a nurse prepared her for a difficult journey, she noted that the child charted an unpredictable course that kept physicians constantly alert.

Following a tense period involving detailed X-rays and severe uncertainty regarding whether the child would survive the holiday season, Phoebe ultimately pulled through. Nevertheless, she encountered subsequent complications, including repeated hospital admissions for persistent chest issues and impaired hearing.

Describing the ordeal as exceptionally traumatic, Goldsmith is currently campaigning for widespread vaccination. The respiratory pathogen typically circulates annually during the winter season, producing mild symptoms in most people but severe illnesses like bronchiolitis and pneumonia in vulnerable demographics. Data indicates that in Wales, seasonal infections among young children under two years old generate thousands of general practitioner appointments and hospital admissions. Similarly, infections among individuals over seventy-five account for substantial medical consultations, hospital admissions, and fatalities annually.

Health authorities emphasize that the immunization is routinely provided year-round to adults aged seventy-five and older, alongside pregnant women from twenty-eight weeks onward to protect newborns. Furthermore, the regional government has broadened the seasonal offering to encompass higher-risk adults aged sixty-five to seventy-four, including immunosuppressed individuals and those suffering from chronic respiratory conditions. Government officials highlighted that these distinct immunizations protect against separate viruses and can definitively determine whether an infection remains mild or necessitates a serious hospital stay.

facts.fact: Jo Goldsmith is urging pregnant women to get vaccinated against RSV after her daughter Phoebe contracted the virus as a newborn.
Phoebe was diagnosed with RSV positive bronchiolitis at five days old on Christmas Eve and was admitted to the high dependency unit.
Phoebe survived but faced longer-term issues including chest problems and hearing affected by the illness.
Nerys Evans, Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, urged people to get vaccinated against Covid-19, flu, and RSV ahead of winter.
RSV typically causes mild coughs and colds but can be serious for infants and older adults.
In Wales, RSV leads to thousands of GP appointments and hospital admissions annually among young children and older adults.
The RSV vaccine is offered routinely to adults aged 75 and over, pregnant women from 28 weeks, and this autumn to higher-risk adults aged 65 to 74.
